summary: A local news opinion piece argues for upgrading street lighting in the neighborhood to address growing nighttime safety concerns. It cites a September 2023 town hall, a survey linking poorly lit streets to minor crime, and expert views on crime prevention and the economy. It describes the Neighborhood Safety Committee's light mapping and LED and smart lighting plans, and urges residents to vote on a funding initiative planned for 2024.
one_line: Residents and officials push for LED and smart street lighting to improve nighttime safety, with a funding vote planned for 2024.
key_facts: A town hall meeting on the evening of September 2, 2023 brought out residents' concerns about nighttime safety; Patricia Gomez described a recent incident that made her feel vulnerable walking home from work.
A survey between September 2023 and December 2023 found poorly lit streets were associated with more minor crimes and growing unease among residents after dark.
Police chief Michael Richardson said "shadowed areas are a cover for criminal activity."
Laura Diaz, an engineer, heads the Neighborhood Safety Committee, which uses a light mapping system to mark spots where streetlamps are missing or inadequate.
On October 15, 2023, Laura Diaz said the aim is to use LED fixtures that give better visibility while reducing energy consumption.
Sociologist Hannah Lee says lighting is about perceived risk as well as actual risk: criminals who believe they are easily visible are deterred.
A Local Business Alliance report, headed by Greg Chen, says upfront lighting costs are high but the return on investment is significant, including a more vibrant evening economy.
City Council member Ana Ramirez presented a budget on November 5th detailing projected costs and expected savings from reduced police needs and higher night-time revenue.
The Neighborhood Safety Committee is exploring motion-sensor lighting and smart lighting systems that adjust dynamically to neighborhood needs.
Jason Kovacs presented a pilot project at a 2023 technology symposium that uses real-time analytics to raise or lower brightness based on street activity.
A community vote scheduled for 2024 will try to secure funding for the project, and organizer Jamal Anderson urges residents to participate.
Photographer Ellen Cho says light is crucial to showing off the community, noting "Everything looks stunning in the golden hour."
